name: Articulate Storyline 360 / Rise 360
tagline: Authoring suite for corporate e-learning: slide-based interactive courses in Storyline, responsive web courses in Rise, both exported to SCORM for an LMS.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The Rise half of this is mostly a static site generator with a quiz block and a progress bar, and an agent can build that in a weekend, SCORM 1.2 manifest included. The SCORM spec is public, the runtime API is about forty lines of JavaScript, and most LMSs only check whether you set lesson_status and a score. Storyline is the part that does not fall over: a timeline, layers, states, variables, triggers, and a drag-and-drop authoring canvas is a real desktop application, not a weekend. Also missing is the content library, millions of licensed photos, icons, and those cursed illustrated office workers, which is a licensing problem rather than a coding one. Build the Rise replacement if you write your own courses; do not try to rebuild Storyline.
coreLoopDIY: Turns a folder of Markdown lessons plus a YAML course file into a responsive self-contained HTML course with quizzes and progress tracking, then zips it as a SCORM 1.2 package an LMS will accept.
requirements: Node 20 and basic command line comfort
Willingness to write course content in Markdown instead of a visual editor
A SCORM test harness (SCORM Cloud free tier or a local LMS) to verify packages
Your own images and media, no stock library included
whatYouLose: The content library: licensed stock photos, icons, characters, templates, and video
Review 360, where stakeholders comment on specific slides and you reply in thread
Storyline's interaction engine: timeline, layers, states, variables, triggers, branching scenarios
Tested compatibility across the LMS zoo, plus xAPI, AICC, and the accessibility conformance work
Translation export and reimport, screen recording, and anyone to call when a client's LMS rejects your package
moatNotes: Storyline's real asset is twenty years of handling LMS edge cases nobody wants to learn about. The content library is a licensing deal you cannot clone.
whyPeopleStillPay: Instructional designers are not paid to maintain a build pipeline, they are paid to ship a compliance course by Friday that works in whatever LMS the client bought in 2014. Articulate is expensive but it absorbs the two worst parts of the job: sourcing visuals that look vaguely professional and producing a package that an unknown LMS will not silently fail to track. Teams also pay for Review 360 because the alternative is a stakeholder emailing you a screenshot with red circles on it. If you author your own content and control your own delivery, almost none of that applies and a static generator is better.
notes: Rise is a static site generator with a certificate at the end; Storyline is a desktop IDE for animation.
prompt:
Build a command line e-learning course generator in Node 20 with TypeScript. No framework, no server, no accounts, no telemetry.

Input: a `course/` folder containing `course.yml` (title, description, author, passing score, lesson order) and one Markdown file per lesson. Markdown supports standard formatting, images from `course/assets/`, and fenced blocks with a `quiz` info string containing YAML for questions (multiple choice, multiple response, true/false), each with options, correct answers, and optional feedback text.

Output: `dist/` containing a fully self-contained responsive HTML course. One page shell, client side routing between lessons, left sidebar lesson list with completion checkmarks, top progress bar, prev/next buttons, keyboard navigation, mobile layout that collapses the sidebar. Inline all CSS and JS into a single bundle with esbuild. Copy assets. No CDN links, no web fonts fetched at runtime, system font stack only.

Quizzes: score on submit, show per question feedback, allow retry, compute a final score across all quizzes, gate a completion screen on the passing score from `course.yml`.

Progress: persist lesson completion and quiz answers in localStorage keyed by course id, so a refresh does not lose state.

Packaging: a `pack` command that emits two artifacts. First, `dist-web/` for plain static hosting. Second, `dist-scorm.zip`, a SCORM 1.2 package with a valid `imsmanifest.xml` (single SCO, the required ADL schema references) and a small runtime wrapper that walks the window hierarchy for the LMS API object, calls LMSInitialize, sets cmi.core.lesson_location on navigation, cmi.core.score.raw and cmi.suspend_data on quiz submit, cmi.core.lesson_status to passed or failed on completion, then LMSCommit and LMSFinish. If no LMS API is found, log once and run in standalone mode instead of crashing.

Also add a `dev` command with file watching and live reload, and a `new` command that scaffolds an example course with two lessons and one quiz so the repo runs immediately after install.

Explicitly out of scope: visual drag and drop editing, timelines, animation, stock asset libraries, xAPI, AICC, multi-user review workflows, translation pipelines.

Write a README with install steps, the `course.yml` schema, the quiz block schema, and a short note on how to test the SCORM zip against SCORM Cloud. Put nothing secret in the repo; if any config is ever needed, read it from `.env` and commit a `.env.example`.
